Chapter Four: Removing Barriers—Creating Space and Focus for Practice.
Even if you’ve got a solid plan and you’re eager to dive in, making steady progress isn’t always as easy as it sounds, is it? Most of the time, the real obstacles aren’t about technique—they’re about your environment and your mindset. Distractions, not enough time, or just the fear of looking silly… any of these can totally throw you off track. But if you really want to get the most out of those first 20 hours of learning, tackling these barriers is a must.
So, where do you start? Well, the first step is setting up an environment that actually helps you focus. That means cutting down on interruptions and making it super easy to begin each session. Sometimes, just a few simple tweaks can make a huge difference:
For example, try setting up a spot just for practice—somewhere away from your phone or the TV, so you’re not tempted to check out. Make specific times for learning and treat them like important appointments you can’t skip. And before you even begin, get all your materials ready. That way, you’re not wasting precious minutes searching for what you need.
These little changes send a clear message to your brain: “Hey, this matters.” They make it way less likely you’ll put things off or just go through the motions.
But there’s something else that gets in the way for a lot of people—the discomfort of being new at something. If you’ve ever held back because you didn’t want to look clueless or mess up, you’re not alone. Honestly, it’s totally normal to feel a bit awkward at first. The trick is to shift your expectations and lean into the learning process.
Think about it: feeling a little clumsy or awkward isn’t a sign you’re failing—it’s proof you’re growing. Every expert started out as a beginner. Those first few steps are supposed to be challenging. If you can accept that being uncomfortable is just part of the ride, it’s so much easier to keep going, even when it feels tough.
Now, let’s talk about time. A lot of folks believe they just don’t have enough hours in the day to pick up something new. But here’s the thing—small, regular efforts add up faster than you’d think. If you can commit to just 20 hours of real, focused practice—spread out over days or weeks—you’ll be amazed at what you can accomplish. The real key? Make learning a routine, not just something you squeeze in when you happen to remember.
If you’re looking for practical ways to knock down those barriers, here are a few tips:
Use a timer to break your practice into short, focused sprints. Keep track of your progress—it’s motivating to see how far you’ve come. And if you can, find a learning buddy or a group. Having someone to share the journey with makes it easier to stay on track.
By tackling both the physical and emotional roadblocks, you make the path to learning so much smoother. Suddenly, it’s not about what’s stopping you—it’s about what you can achieve when you keep showing up, day after day.
